archetype.name: Rookie Developmental (emergency fill-in)
archetype.definition: An undrafted 25-year-old rookie pressed into duty during Lamar Jackson's thumb injury, running a short, horizontal version of the offense with no proven skill to build around yet.

report.headline: Two outings, no answers: a checkdown offense that turned the ball over
report.take:
Joe Fagnano is the Ravens' emergency quarterback in a season that has burned through four starters. He came on for 40% of the snaps in Week 8 at Buffalo, started on four days' rest against Jacksonville in Week 9, and then gave way to Tyler Huntley and Jacoby Brissett. He is listed QB2 as of November 24. His 45 dropbacks are a small sample, but the picture is consistent. His -0.515 EPA per dropback ranks 53rd of 55 qualifiers, his 3.87 yards per attempt and 0.77 adjusted net yards per dropback both rank last, and three interceptions on 39 throws put his INT rate at 7.7%, against a league average of 2.5%.

The damage comes from what the offense asked him to do, and from what he did with it. His intended air yards sit at 3.89 and his throws average 5.32 yards short of the sticks. Eleven of his 39 attempts came behind the line, and those screens and swings lost -0.822 EPA a play with an 18% success rate. On 33 throws under 10 air yards, his completion rate was 14.4 points below expected. That is not a coverage problem. Those are easy throws that weren't completed or didn't gain anything. Meanwhile the six passes he pushed 10-19 yards were roughly neutral, with a 50% success rate. That is too few to call a skill, but it suggests the conservative plan cost more than it protected.

The two games differ in instructive ways. At Buffalo he was under siege: pressured on 52% of dropbacks, a 23.8% bad-throw rate, three sacks and a lost fumble. Against Jacksonville, now the No. 2 defense, he was pressured only 25% of the time and his bad-throw rate fell to 6.7%. He threw more accurately but even shorter, at 2.4 intended air yards, and still threw two interceptions. All three of his picks went to the left side. His nine targets to Zay Flowers produced -14.9 EPA, most of his total damage, which looks like a timing and trust problem with his best receiver, not a pass-catcher issue. Mark Andrews was the only frequent target he moved the chains with.

Where this goes is mostly out of his hands. Baltimore turned to two other quarterbacks after his start, and Jackson has a reported chance to return around Week 16. Fagnano is most likely a clipboard holder from here. If he does play, the evidence says the offense has to let him throw past the sticks rather than keep him to throws behind the line.

strengths.title: Held up when allowed downfield
strengths.body: His six throws of 10-19 air yards came out near neutral, with a 50% success rate and completions right at expectation. That is the only depth where he wasn't a drain. It is a hint, not a finding, at six attempts. But it argues the ultra-short plan did him no favors.

strengths.title: Cleaner mechanics in a clean pocket
strengths.body: In his Week 9 start, Jacksonville pressured him on only 25% of dropbacks. His bad-throw rate dropped to 6.7%, from 23.8% the week before. That is a real improvement in ball placement when he wasn't hurried. The issue that day was decision-making and depth, not accuracy.

strengths.title: Andrews as a reliable outlet
strengths.body: Mark Andrews was the only one of his regular targets to post positive EPA. He did it on six looks. Tight-end throws over the middle are the most natural fit for a young quarterback working short.

concerns.title: Short throws that went nowhere
concerns.body: With 3.89 intended air yards and throws 5.32 yards short of the sticks, the offense lived on screens and checkdowns. He then missed them: -0.822 EPA a play behind the line and completions 14.4 points under expectation on throws under 10 yards. Part of this is a conservative emergency game plan. But the execution on the easiest throws was poor, and that is a real flaw.

concerns.title: Turnovers, especially toward Flowers
concerns.body: His 7.7% interception rate ranks 53rd of 55, and he added two turnover-worthy fumbles. All three picks went to the left side, and Flowers targets alone produced -14.9 EPA. That pattern reads as forcing throws to his top receiver without the timing built in practice reps. It may ease with reps, but he isn't getting them.

concerns.title: Coming apart under pressure
concerns.body: Buffalo pressured him on 52% of dropbacks. He sprayed the ball, took three sacks and lost a fumble. His season pressure rate of 41.9% partly reflects a Ravens line that ranks 24th in hit rate allowed. Still, a 9.3% sack rate shows he doesn't yet get the ball out when the pocket collapses.

trend.note: Both appearances were deeply negative, at -10.4 and -11.7 pass EPA. Accuracy improved in his start, but the depth and turnovers didn't. Baltimore has since started Huntley and Brissett, so the path has gone sideways into a backup role.

nextGame.headline: Likely on the sideline; a rough spot if he plays
nextGame.body:
Fagnano is listed QB2 heading into Houston, and Brissett started last week, so he probably plays only in relief. If he does see the field, Houston is a bad match for his profile. The Texans rank 3rd in sack rate and 6th in success rate allowed, which punishes exactly the short, low-margin offense he ran. Their weakness is the explosive pass: they rank 31st in explosive pass rate allowed, but he has barely thrown past 10 yards. The Book has Baltimore as a 6.5-point underdog. Houston's passing offense ranks 8th, and Baltimore's defense is 30th against deep passes, so a trailing script is plausible. That is where he has been at his worst.

Houston will be without edge rusher Danielle Hunter, a 76%-snap starter. That removes the biggest pass-rush threat and could ease the pressure that wrecked his Buffalo outing. Defensive tackle Sheldon Rankins is questionable. On Baltimore's side, Lamar Jackson remains on IR with a possible Week 16 return, which is what keeps Fagnano a backup rather than a starter. The retractable-roof forecast is mild.

keyMatchups.title: Houston's sack rate vs. his pocket
keyMatchups.body: Houston gets home on 8.9% of dropbacks, third-best in the league. Fagnano's pressure-to-sack rate is already 22.2%. Hunter's absence helps, but this is still a front that feasts on quarterbacks who hold the ball and then check it down.

keyMatchups.title: Explosive-pass leak he can't exploit
keyMatchups.body: Houston allows explosive passes at the second-worst rate in the league. Fagnano's offense has been built around throws behind the line and in the flat. Unless the plan changes to let him push it, that weakness goes unused.

keyMatchups.title: Trailing script and tight-end coverage
keyMatchups.body: When he was down 9 or more, he posted -0.586 EPA a play. Houston has also held top tight ends 3 PPR points under their averages, which squeezes Andrews, the one target who worked for him.

nextGame.watch: Whether Fagnano takes any snaps at all, and if he does, whether Baltimore lets him throw beyond the sticks.

restOfSeason.body:
The realistic expectation is a backup role. Baltimore has cycled to Huntley and Brissett since his start, and Jackson is targeting a return around Week 16, so Fagnano's path to more starts runs through further injuries or a benching. If he is called on again, expect a short-passing plan with low yardage and a high turnover risk against all but soft defenses. The 7.7% interception rate on 39 throws should come down simply because that is an extreme figure on small volume. The completion and EPA problems on easy throws look more like who he is right now.

There is a modest upside case. His accuracy cleaned up when he had time, and his few intermediate throws held up. With a week of first-team reps and a game plan that attacks past the sticks, he could reach replacement-level efficiency. Nothing in two appearances shows a quarterback who can carry the offense.
swingFactors: Whether Brissett or Huntley holds the job
Play-calling that lets him throw past the sticks

confidence.note: 45 dropbacks over two games, one start on short rest, and an uncertain role.
